A sealed, full-body garment, usually with an attachable helmet, which maintains air pressure or mechanical pressure around the body of an astronaut or aviator to compensate for the low density of the air at high altitudes.
x: Have you fur pressure-suits?
The chances for survival would be greatly increased if one member of the crew in a punctured ship was wearing a pressure suit.

s.d: a unit measuring force per unit area
cook in a pressure cooker
mechanical system of lubricating internal combustion engines in which a pump forces oil into the engine bearings
wash before painting to remove old paint and mildew
x: pressure-wash the house

prestidigitation.e: From French prestidigitation, from French preste (“nimble, quick”) + Latin digitus (“finger”) + French -ation (process suffix). The word has a different origin from prestige, even though this in the past has meant “delusion, illusion, trick”.

s.d: manual dexterity in the execution of tricks
(uncountable) A performance of or skill in performing magic or conjuring tricks with the hands.
x: My favorite prestidigitation was when he pulled the live dove out of that tiny scarf.

s.d: (uncountable) A show of skill or deceitful cleverness.
x: His writing was peppered with verbal tricks and prestidigitation.

s.d: someone who performs magic tricks to amuse an audience
One who performs feats of prestidigitation; a sleight-of-hand artist.

prestige.e: From French prestige (“illusion, fascination, enchantment, prestige”), from Latin praestīgium (“a delusion, an illusion”). Despite the phonetic similarities and the old meaning of “delusion, illusion, trick”, the word has a different root than prestidigitator (“conjurer”) and prestidigitation.

s.d: a high standing achieved through success or influence or wealth etc.
x: he wanted to achieve power and prestige

s.d: (uncountable) The quality of how good the reputation of something or someone is, how favourably something or someone is regarded.
x: Oxford has a university of very high prestige.
But in such an instance a false belief will appear with all the prestige of the latest scientific knowledge supporting it.

s.d: (obsolete, uncountable) Delusion; illusion; trick.
x: That faith which, we are told, was founded on a rock, impregnable to the assaults of men and demons; to the sophisms of infidelity, and the prestiges of imposture!

s.d: (uncountable) The act of starting over at an earlier point in a video game with some type of bonus or reward.
x: When Season 1 starts, so does prestige for anyone who has reached level 55.
There's new Omnimovement, changes to progression and prestige, the option to share your best weapon builds.

s.d: A level, rank, or tier corresponding to prestige.
x: With dozens of custom enchantments, unique prestiges, and a player-driven economy, ManaCube offers a rich and immersive Prison experience.

s.d: To start over at an earlier point in a video game with some type of bonus or reward.
x: This seriously depends on the prerequisites, but most chars will already have a +1 bow by the time they're thinking of prestiging - or will this stack with the equipment's magic?
Reached level 50 and prestiged which I have never had the inclination to do in any game before.

s.d: Regarded as relatively prestigious; often, considered the standard language or language variety, or a part of such a variety.
x: Furthermore there is in each area a well recognized standard, known by a single name, which although often linguistically distinct from local dialects, has served as the prestige form for some time.
The 3rd person plural -ą ending is phonetically [ow̃] or [om], depending on the dialect. However, [ow̃] is the prestige form.

prestigious.e: Attested since the 1540s; Latin praestigiosus (“full of tricks”), praestigiae (“juggler's tricks”), possibly an alteration of praestringō (“to blindfold, to dazzle”), from prae- (“before”) with stringō (“to bind or tie”); equivalent to prestige + -ious. Unstressed /ɛ/ is retained by analogy with prestige.

s.d: having an illustrious reputation; respected

a prestigious author

s.d: exerting influence by reason of high status or prestige
x: a prestigious professor at a prestigious university

s.d: a high standing achieved through success or influence or wealth etc.

s.d: (uncountable) The state or condition of being prestigious.

s.d: (of tempo) as fast as possible

s.d: Very quickly.
x: A delegation of Norman gentry boldly requesting in 1771 the calling of the Normandy estates (which had been abolished in 1666) was despatched prestissimo to the Bastille.

suddenly as if by a magic trick

s.d: at a very fast tempo (faster than allegro)
Very fast or quickly; a directive for the musician(s) to play in a very quick tempo.

presume.e: From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).

s.d: take to be the case or to be true; accept without verification or proof
x: I assume his train was late

s.d: take upon oneself; act presumptuously, without permission
x: How dare you call my lawyer?

s.d: constitute reasonable evidence for
x: A restaurant bill presumes the consumption of food

s.d: take liberties or act with too much confidence
To be so presumptuous as (to do something) without proper authority or permission [with to (+ infinitive)].
x: I don't want to pretend to be an authority on this line of business, so I would never presume to tell you how to run your own company.

s.d: (archaic) To perform, do (something) without authority; to lay claim to without permission.
x: Don't make the decision yourself and presume too much.

s.d: To assume or suggest to be true (without proof); to take for granted, to suppose.
x: Paw-prints in the snow allow us to presume a visit from next door's cat.
Dr. Livingstone, I presume?

s.d: To take as a premise; to assume for the sake of argument.
x: If we presume that human cloning may one day become a mundane, everyday reality, then maybe it's time to start thinking more positively about our soon-to-arrive genetically engineered pseudo-siblings.

s.d: To impose (on) for one's advantage; to be presumptuous; to take advantage (of); to take liberties (with) [with on or upon].
x: Thanks, but I can't accept the money; I would not want to presume on the generosity of a stranger'

Presume not on thy heart when mine is slain;
Thou gavest me thine, not to give back again.

s.d: Of or relating to property or ownership.
x: proprietary rights

s.d: Owning something; having ownership.
x: the proprietary class

s.d: Created or manufactured exclusively by the owner or licensee of intellectual property rights, as with a patent or trade secret.
x: The continuous profitability of the company is based on its many proprietary products.
It was reported that the recipes for the secret sauce and grinder sandwiches were proprietary, known only to the current president of the corporation and the former owner of the restaurant.

s.d: Nonstandard and controlled by one particular organization.
x: a proprietary extension to the HTML standard for Web page structure

s.d: Privately owned.
x: a proprietary lake;   a proprietary chapel

s.d: Possessive, jealous, or territorial.
a colony given to a proprietor to govern (in 17th century)
a drug that has a trade name and is protected by a patent (can be produced and sold only by the company holding the patent)
(law) someone who owns (is legal possessor of) a business
x: he is the owner of a chain of restaurants

s.d: An owner.
x: Here the proprietor has had the good sense of holding on to the good old fashion of giving his customers their moneyworth of good wines and liquors.

s.d: A sole owner of an unincorporated business, also called a sole proprietor.
One of the owners of an unincorporated business, a partner.
One or more persons to whom a colonial territory is assigned, like a fief, including its administration.
x: From 10 September 1621 till 12 June 1632, Sir William Alexander, styled Earl of Stirling and Viscount of Canada, was proprietor of the Scottish colony Nova Scotia.

s.d: an unincorporated business owned by a single person who is responsible for its liabilities and entitled to its profits
(uncountable) The state of being a proprietor; ownership.
a certificate showing who is responsible in an individually owned business

proprietress.e:
Etymology tree

From proprietor + -ess.

s.d: a woman proprietor
(dated) A female proprietor.
x: In addition, the proprietress is a Nazi. We barely escaped with our lives.

propriety.e: From late Middle English proprietee, propretee, propriete (“ownership”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman propreté, Middle French proprieté, from Latin proprietās. By surface analysis, prop(e)r + -iety. Doublet of property.

s.d: correct or appropriate behavior
(obsolete, uncountable) The particular character or essence of someone or something; individuality.
(obsolete, uncountable) A characteristic; an attribute.
(archaic, uncountable) A piece of land owned by someone; someone's property.
(obsolete, uncountable) More generally, something owned by someone; a possession.
x: I was fearful of giving You a very sensible Disgust, in making You seem the Propriety of one Man, when You know Yourself ordained for the Comfort and Refreshment of Multitudes.

s.d: (uncountable) The fact of possessing something; ownership.
x: This ſweet word, I will be your God, implies, 1. Propriety, that all that is in God ſhall be ours; his love ours, his Spirit ours, his mercy ours.

s.d: (archaic, uncountable) Correct language or pronunciation.
x: Thoſe who ought to be the guardians of propriety are often the perverters of it. Hence Accidence for Accidents, Prepoſtor for Prepoſitor and Conſtur for Conſtrue[…]

s.d: (uncountable) Suitability, fitness; the quality of being appropriate.
x: I find such a pleasure, sir, in obeying your commands, that I take care to observe them without ever debating their propriety.
Now, if we may, with propriety, refer to the people one question, why may we not, with equal propriety, refer another?

s.d: (uncountable) Correctness in behaviour and morals; good manners, seemliness.
x: Elinor then ventured to doubt the propriety of her receiving such a present from a man so little, or at least so lately known to her.

proprioception.e: From proprioceptor, from Latin proprius (“one's own”) + reception. Coined by British neurophysiologist Charles Scott Sherrington in 1906.

s.d: the ability to sense the position and location and orientation and movement of the body and its parts
(uncountable) The sense of the position of parts of the body, relative to other neighbouring parts of the body.
x: […] it is achieved through a neuromuscular feedback system known as proprioception or kinaesthetic awareness, as well as through an auditory control system in which the ear monitors the sound and makes […]

Sometimes referred to as our sixth sense, proprioception is what helps high-level athletes take a penalty without looking at the ball, or orient themselves in the air while doing a twisting somersault.

proprioceptive.e: Coined by English neurophysiologist Charles Sherrington in 1906, originally in the spelling proprio-ceptive, from proprius + clipped receptive.

s.d: of or relating to proprioception
Of or pertaining to proprioception.
x: [I]t’s becoming clear, as our understanding of it improves, that improving or maintaining our proprioceptive ability is key to our quality of life as we age.

proprioceptor.e: Coined by English neurophysiologist Charles Sherrington in 1906, originally in the spelling proprio-ceptor, from proprius + clipped receptor.

s.d: special nerve endings in the muscles and tendons and other organs that respond to stimuli regarding the position and movement of the body
A nerve ending that functions as a sensory receptor in muscles, tendons, joints and the inner ear; they respond to movement and position
the amide of propionic acid (C2H5CONH2)
proper respect
x: I have to give my props to the governor for the way he handled the problem

s.d: (obsolete) A game of chance using four seashells (each called a prop).

propulsion.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsio, propulsionis, from the past participle of Latin propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

s.d: a propelling force
the act of propelling
(uncountable) The process of propelling, driving, or pushing, typically forward or onward; a propulsive force or impulse.
(uncountable) That which propels.
x: However, nuclear propulsion provides a very high specific impulse and consistent, long duration energy source.
This propulsion provides an initial velocity for the vehicle in a short time span.

s.d: a system that provides a propelling or driving force

propulsive.e: Formed from Latin prōpulsus with the suffix -ive.

s.d: having the power to propel
x: propulsive coefficient

s.d: tending to or capable of propelling
x: propellant fuel for submarines
the faster a jet plane goes the greater its propulsive efficiency

s.d: Of or pertaining to propulsion
Serving to propel
female member of the stage crew in charge of properties
A woman responsible for looking after the props in a theater

From the chemical prefix propyl-, from propylic or directly from earlier French propylique, from prop(ionique) + -yle + -ique, where -yle, as in French méthylène, is from ὕλη (húlē, “wood, substance”).

s.d: the monovalent organic group C3H7- obtained from propane
Either of two isomeric univalent hydrocarbon radicals, C₃H₇, formally derived from propane by the loss of a hydrogen atom.
a clear colorless volatile liquid (alcohol) used as a solvent and antiseptic
(uncountable) Synonym of 1-propanol.
the monovalent organic group C3H7- obtained from propane
the monovalent organic group C3H7- obtained from propane

propylene.e: Coined by John Williams Reynolds in 1851, from French propionique + -ylene

s.d: a flammable gas obtained by cracking petroleum; used in organic synthesis
(uncountable) The organic chemical compound propene. An alkene which is a colorless gaseous (at room temperature and pressure) hydrocarbon with the chemical formula C₃H₆.

a sweet colorless, viscous, hygroscopic liquid used as an antifreeze and in brake fluid and also as a humectant in cosmetics and personal care items although it can be absorbed through the skin with harmful effects
(uncountable) α-propyleneglycol, 1,2-propanediol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂OH, a thick oily liquid, used as an antifreeze and in many industrial applications
propandiol, any propane chain with two alcohol functional groups attached
a crystalline compound used as an antithyroid drug in the treatment of goiter
(uncountable) A thioamide drug, used to treat hyperthyroidism by decreasing the amount of thyroid hormone produced by the thyroid gland, which is associated with a risk of agranulocytosis.

prorate.e: American English derivation from pro rata, from Latin pro (“according to”) + ratus (“calculated”).

s.d: make a proportional settlement or distribution
divide or assess proportionally
x: The rent was prorated for the rest of the month

s.d: To divide proportionately, especially by day; to divide pro rata.
the proportional limitation of production or distribution of something (e.g. crude oil or natural gas) to some fractional part of the total capacity of each producer

(uncountable) In budgeting, the proportional distribution or allocation of parameters, such as noise power and transmission losses, among a number of tandem-connected items, such as equipment, cables, links, or trunks, in order to balance the performance of communications circuits.
(uncountable) In a telephone switching center, the distribution or allocation of equipment or components proportionally among a number of functions, to provide a requisite grade of service.

(uncountable) In the insurance industry, the act of taking money that is currently due from the insurance company and moving it to the patient, knowing that the dollar amount being moved is due from the patient as a deductible, coinsurance, or copayment amount.

prorogation.e: From Anglo-Norman prorogation, Middle French prorogation, and their source, Latin prōrogātiō (“extension, postponement”).

s.d: discontinuation of the meeting (of a legislative body) without dissolving it
(uncountable) Causing something to last longer or remain in effect longer; prolongation, continuance.
(uncountable) The action of proroguing an assembly, especially a parliament; discontinuance of meetings for a given period of time, without dissolution.
(uncountable) The period of such a discontinuance between two sessions of a legislative body.
(archaic, uncountable) Deferral to a later time; postponement.

prorogue.e: From Old French proroger, proroguer, from Latin prōrogō (“prolong, defer”).

s.d: hold back to a later time
x: let's postpone the exam

s.d: adjourn by royal prerogative; without dissolving the legislative body
To suspend (a parliamentary session) or to discontinue the meetings of (an assembly, parliament etc.) without formally ending the session.
(archaic) To defer.
(obsolete) To prolong or extend.
x: Mirth[…]prorogues life, whets the wit, makes the body young, lively, and fit for any manner of employment.
The King settled to prorogue Parliament until the Christmas holidays, and to do nothing else for the present.

prosaic.e: From Middle French prosaïque, from Medieval Latin prosaicus (“in prose”), from Latin prosa (“prose”), from prorsus (“straightforward, in prose”), from Old Latin provorsus (“straight ahead”), from pro- (“forward”) + vorsus (“turned”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn, to bend”).

s.d: not fanciful or imaginative
x: local guides describe the history of various places in matter-of-fact tones
a prosaic and unimaginative essay

s.d: lacking wit or imagination
x: a pedestrian movie plot

s.d: not challenging; dull and lacking excitement
x: an unglamorous job greasing engines

s.d: Pertaining to or having the characteristics of prose.
x: The tenor of Eliot's prosaic work differs greatly from that of his poetry.

s.d: Straightforward; matter-of-fact; lacking the feeling or elegance of poetry.
x: I was simply making the prosaic point that we are running late.

s.d: Overly plain, simple or commonplace, to the point of being boring.
x: His account of the incident was so prosaic that I nodded off while reading it.
She lived a prosaic life.

s.d: in a matter-of-fact manner

s.d: In a prosaic manner; straightforwardly.

proscenium.e: From Latin proscaenium (“in front of the scenery”), from Ancient Greek προσκήνιον (proskḗnion), from πρό (pró, “before”) + σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene building”).

s.d: the part of a modern theater stage between the curtain and the orchestra (i.e., in front of the curtain)
the wall that separates the stage from the auditorium in a modern theater
The stage area between the curtain and the orchestra.
x: It looks like a film, a meticulous, detailed, visually balanced wide-screen Wes Anderson one. There’s no proscenium, no stage, no wings, no audience.

s.d: The stage area immediately in front of the scene building.
The row of columns at the front of the scene building, at first directly behind the circular orchestra but later upon a stage.
x: The front of the scene-building and of the parascenia came to be decorated with a row of columns, the proscenium (πρό, "before"+σκηνή).

s.d: A proscenium arch.
x: Screamers trumpeted from the roof of the supermarket, white storks rattled their bills as their surveyed the town from the proscenium of the filling-station.

s.d: the arch over the opening in the proscenium wall
The arch that frames a theater stage, and separates it from the auditorium.
x: I started using filmic grammar, rather than traditional proscenium arch grammar, because I worked in the round primarily.

s.d: the wall that separates the stage from the auditorium in a modern theater

prosciutto.e: Borrowed from Italian prosciutto (meaning 'ham', in general), from asciutto, with a change of prefix, or from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from per + Latin exsūctus.

s.d: Italian salt-cured ham usually sliced paper thin
(uncountable) A dry-cured ham from Italy, thinly sliced.
x: He also manages to extract refined performances from overseasoned prosciutti like […]
In front of him, on a low table, a plate of prosciutto, olives and cheese.

s.d: a type of prosciutto ham.
x: A number of regions have their own variations of prosciutto, each with degrees of protected status, but the most prized are the Prosciutto di Parma PDO from the Emilia-Romagna region and the Prosciutto di San Daniele PDO from the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region.

s.d: command against
x: I forbid you to call me late at night
Mother vetoed the trip to the chocolate store

s.d: To forbid or prohibit.
x: The law proscribes driving a car while intoxicated.

s.d: To denounce.
x: The word ‘ain't’ is proscribed by many authorities.

s.d: To banish or exclude.
x: Many Roman citizens were proscribed for taking part in rebellions.

s.d: excluded from use or mention
x: forbidden fruit
in our house dancing and playing cards were out

s.d: Forbidden or prohibited.

proscription.e: From Middle English proscripcion, from Latin prōscrīptiō, from prōscrībō (originally "publish in writing"), from prō- and scrībō (“write”).

s.d: a decree that prohibits something
rejection by means of an act of banishing or proscribing someone
(uncountable) A prohibition.
(uncountable) Decree of condemnation toward one or more persons, especially in the Roman antiquity.
x: He was wholly unopposed, for the boldest spirits had fallen in battle, or in the proscription [...]

s.d: (uncountable) The act of proscribing, or its result.
(uncountable) A decree or law that prohibits.

prose.e:
From Middle English prose, from Old French prose, from Latin prōsa (“straightforward”) from the term prōsa ōrātiō (“a straightforward speech – i.e. without the ornaments of verse”).
further etymology and related terms
The term prōsa (“straightforward”), a colloquial form of prorsa (“straight forwards”), the feminine form prorsus (“straight forwards”), from Old Latin prōvorsus (“moving straight ahead”), from pro- (“forward”) + vorsus (“turned”), form of vertō (“to turn”). Compare verse.

s.d: ordinary writing as distinguished from verse
matter of fact, commonplace, or dull expression
(uncountable) Language, particularly written language, not intended as poetry.
x: Though known mostly for her prose, she also produced a small body of excellent poems.

s.d: (uncountable) Language which evinces little imagination or animation; dull and commonplace discourse.
x: ...the vehicle is plodding prose, but the effect is none the less poignant. And in regard to this I may say that in a hundred places in Trollope the extremity of pathos is reached by the homeliest means.

s.d: (uncountable) A hymn with no regular meter, sometimes introduced into the Mass.
To write or repeat in a dull, tedious, or prosy way.
x:
Pray, do not prose, good Ethelbert, but speak;
What is your purpose?

s.d: prose that resembles poetry

A literary text written in the manner of prose—without the fixed lines, rhyme, and meter often characteristic of poetry—but nonetheless clearly possessing some of the distinctive attributes of poetry, such as lyrical language, evocation of feeling, vivid imagery, metaphor, and linguistic devices like assonance or alliteration.
x: "He is the author of a very wild Mystery, or dramatic prose-poem, in which the Ocean, Mont-Blanc, and the Cathedral of Strassburg have parts to play."
In form and spirit the book is unique, a simple romantic narrative transmuted by sheer glow of beauty into a prose poem.

prosecute.e: Borrowed from Latin prōsecūtus, perfect participle of prōsequor. Doublet of pursue, from Old French. Compare also persecute.

s.d: conduct a prosecution in a court of law
bring a criminal action against (in a trial)
x: The State of California prosecuted O.J. Simpson

s.d: carry out or participate in an activity; be involved in
x: She pursued many activities
They engaged in a discussion

s.d: To start criminal proceedings against.
x: to prosecute a man for trespass, or for a riot
To acquit themſelves and proſecute their foes

s.d: To charge, try.
x: The Vigilante is prosecuted in Federal Court under a lynch bill and winds up in a Federal Nut House specially designed for the containment of ghosts […]

s.d: To seek to obtain by legal process.
x: to prosecute a right or a claim in a court of law

s.d: To pursue something to the end.
x: to prosecute a scheme, hope, or an investigation
I am beloved of beauteous Hermia; / Why should not I, then, prosecute my right?

s.d: a government official who conducts criminal prosecutions on behalf of the state

A public officer charged with carrying on the prosecution or representing the state in criminal proceedings and, in some jurisdictions, instituting or representing the state in civil or administrative proceedings.
a government official who conducts criminal prosecutions on behalf of the state

prosecution.e: From Middle French prosecution and its etymon Late Latin prōsecutio, from Latin prōsequor (“follow, pursue”), from pro- (“onward”) + sequor (“follow”, whence English sequel). Compare persecution, and see more at prosecute. By surface analysis, prosecute + -ion.

s.d: the institution and conduct of legal proceedings against a defendant for criminal behavior
the lawyers acting for the state to put the case against the defendant
the continuance of something begun with a view to its completion
(uncountable) The act of prosecuting a scheme or endeavor.
x: The prosecution of the war fell to Winston Churchill.
Many apartheid perpetrators escaped prosecution for their persecution of black Africans and political dissidents.

s.d: (uncountable) The institution of legal proceedings (particularly criminal) against a person.
(uncountable) The prosecuting party.
(uncountable) In many countries, a legal body and institution, usually part of the state apparatus, empowered to perform prosecution. Prosecutor's Office. See Prosecutor.
x: Backed by public outrage, the prosecution requested the death penalty to be imposed on the murderer.

prosecutor.e: First use appears c. 1542, from Medieval Latin prosecutor, from prōsequor (English prosecute). By surface analysis, prosecute + -or.

s.d: a government official who conducts criminal prosecutions on behalf of the state
A prosecuting attorney.
x: Annie Jay was the Wisconsin government prosecutor in the trial of a man for forging his client's signature.
It sat by mutely while Jack Abramoff, the superlobbyist, spun schemes that eroded public trust, until prosecutors had to move in.

s.d: A person, as a complainant, victim, or chief witness, who institutes prosecution in a criminal proceeding.
x: The prosecutor got the witness to admit he was lying.

proselyte.e: From Old French proselite, from Late Latin proselytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”) (from πρός (prós, “to, towards”) and the stem -ηλυ- of ἐλήλυθα (elḗlutha), perfect of ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “come”)), translation of Hebrew גר (ger) in the Septuagint translation of the Torah (e.g., Exodus 12:49); also used in Matthew 23:15, Acts 2:10, Acts 6:5.

s.d: a new convert; especially a gentile converted to Judaism
One who has converted to a religion or doctrine, especially a gentile converted to Judaism.
x: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.
That evening the young nun lay exhausted between life and death in a brain fever, while all Naples was ringing with the faith, beauty, and fervour of the English proselyte.

s.d: To proselytize.

s.d: convert to another faith or religion
To advertise one’s religious beliefs; to convert (someone) to one’s own faith or religious movement or encourage them to do so.
x: One of these [people] whom they endeavour to proselytize.
“I am not sent here to proselytize. My church is not in that business.”

s.d: To advertise a non-religious belief, way of living, cause, point of view, (scientific) hypothesis, social or other position, political party, or other organization; to convince someone to join such a cause or organization or support such a position; to recruit someone.
x: He has strong political views, and an annoying habit of proselytizing at parties.

Previously I promised not to proselytize miserism, but now I want to renege a little on that promise. If your family income is anywhere near average, you can scrimp and save and cut back for maybe two to four years […]

s.d: a course of study like a graduate seminar but often open to advanced undergraduates.
x: They, in turn, would invite me to join a proseminar where I spent a semester developing a dissertation on American bandit crime with Eric Hobsbawm.

s.d: A seminar that is open to (and accessible to) upper level undergraduates; contrasts with a graduate seminar (for graduate students only), which assumes more background.

prosencephalon.e: From pros- + encephalon. pros- is from Ancient Greek πρόσω (prósō).

s.d: the anterior portion of the brain; the part of the brain that develops from the anterior part of the neural tube
The forebrain.
x: Holonym: encephalon

s.d: in a prosy manner
x: somewhat prosily and repetitively expounded

A primate that is not a monkey or an ape, generally nocturnal with large eyes and ears. Such primates were formerly grouped in the suborder Prosimii, but are now considered a paraphyletic group and not a clade.
Of or from the prosimian suborder of primates.
commonplaceness as a consequence of being humdrum and not exciting

The quality of being beneficial to all parties and consistent with community laws and mores.

s.d: (uncountable) The quality of being prosocial.
x: DeBruine ( 2004 a) provided preliminary evidence that facial resemblance has a different impact in the domain of mate choice than in the domain of prosociality.

A processional hymn.
x: Alcman composed various kinds of poems in various metres; Parthenia (maidens’ songs), hymns, paeans, prosodia (processionals), and love-songs, of which he was considered the inventor.
